lessons.title: View Identity & the Render Loop
lessons.body:
SwiftUI views are **value types** — plain structs. Every time your state changes, SwiftUI calls `body` again and produces a fresh struct. It then **diffs the view tree** against the previous one to decide what actually needs updating on screen.

This diff relies on **identity**. SwiftUI uses two kinds:

- **Structural identity** — the view's type and position in the hierarchy. Most views get this automatically.
- **Explicit identity** — assigned with the `.id()` modifier. Use this to tell SwiftUI "this is a new view" even if it appears in the same position.

A view's **lifetime** is tied to its identity. As long as identity is stable, SwiftUI keeps the view alive and preserves its `@State`. The moment identity changes, SwiftUI destroys the old view and creates a fresh one — **all local state resets**.

This is why `ForEach` requires a stable `id` parameter. If ids change (e.g., using array indices on a mutable list), SwiftUI may destroy and recreate views unnecessarily, causing flickering and lost state.

```swift
// Stable string ids — state survives reorders
ForEach(items, id: \.id) { item in
    ItemRow(item: item)
}
```

Prefer `Identifiable` conformance or a stable, unique property as the id. Avoid using array indices when the array can be reordered or filtered.

quickCheck.prompt: What happens to a view's state when its identity changes?
quickCheck.explanation: Identity is the key SwiftUI uses to find existing state storage. A new identity means SwiftUI treats it as a brand-new view — no state is carried over.

options.text: It is destroyed and recreated from scratch
State is preserved across identity changes
State is migrated to the new identity
A runtime error is thrown

lessons.title: State Management — @State, @Binding, @Observable, @Environment

quickCheck.explanation: @Binding is a derived reference — it points into a parent's @State storage. The child can read and write, but the parent owns the value and its lifetime.

options.text: A two-way reference to a parent's @State
An independent copy of a value
A strong reference to an ObservableObject
A persistent storage entry

lessons.title: Layout System — Stacks, Frames, GeometryReader
lessons.body:
SwiftUI's layout follows a clear protocol: **parent offers size, child chooses its own size, parent places it**. Understanding this removes most layout mysteries.

**The three stacks:**
- `HStack` — horizontal axis
- `VStack` — vertical axis
- `ZStack` — z-axis (front to back layering)

**`.frame()`** lets you propose a specific size to a child or constrain it. `minWidth/maxWidth` create flexible ranges.

**`Spacer`** expands to fill available space along the stack's axis, pushing siblings apart.

**`layoutPriority`** controls which views shrink last when space is tight. Higher priority = last to compress (default is 0).

```swift
VStack {
    Text("Header")
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
    Spacer()
    HStack {
        Text("Left").layoutPriority(1)
        Text("Right side with more content")
    }
    .padding()
    .frame(height: 44)
}
```

**`GeometryReader`** gives you the parent's offered size at render time. It's powerful but has a cost: it expands to fill all available space and can cause unexpected layouts. Use it only when you genuinely need dynamic sizing — not as a default wrapper.

Common pitfall: wrapping a simple view in `GeometryReader` just to get the screen width. Prefer `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` or environment values instead.

quickCheck.prompt: Which stack layers views along the z-axis (front to back)?
quickCheck.explanation: ZStack places its children on top of one another along the z-axis. The last child in the closure appears on top visually.

options.text: ZStack
HStack
VStack
LazyVStack

questions.prompt: What triggers SwiftUI to re-render a view's body?
questions.explanation: SwiftUI tracks which state the body accessed during the last render. Only changes to those specific dependencies trigger a new render — unread state is invisible.

options.text: Any property on the view changes
Only @State, @Binding, @Observable, or @Environment dependencies that the body reads change
A timer fires
The app becomes active

questions.prompt: What is the difference between @State and @Binding?
questions.explanation: @State is the source of truth — the view owns the storage. @Binding is a reference into that storage, letting child views read and write the parent's value.

options.text: @State is for classes; @Binding is for structs
@State owns the value and is local to a view; @Binding is a derived two-way reference to a parent's state
They are interchangeable
@Binding owns the value; @State is a read-only projection

questions.explanation: @Observable auto-tracks exactly which properties a view reads, publishing changes only for those — no per-property @Published boilerplate and finer-grained updates.

options.text: ObservableObject is faster; @Observable is for legacy compatibility
@Observable uses a macro for automatic fine-grained observation without needing @Published on every property
They work identically — @Observable is just a shorthand
@Observable requires @StateObject; ObservableObject works with @State

questions.prompt: Views in SwiftUI are value types. What does this mean for state?
questions.explanation: The struct itself is recreated every render cycle, but @State and @Binding are backed by SwiftUI's persistent storage — keyed to the view's identity, not the struct instance.

options.text: State must be stored in a class to persist
SwiftUI manages state storage separately — the struct is recreated on each render but @State persists via SwiftUI's storage
Views cannot have mutable state
Value-type views are always re-created from scratch, losing all state

questions.explanation: @State persists across re-renders and triggers body re-evaluation when mutated — each tap increments count and SwiftUI updates the label automatically.

options.text: A button that increments a counter and updates its label each tap
A button that always shows 'Count: 0'
Compile error — @State cannot be used in a struct
A button that crashes on tap

questions.explanation: .onAppear runs once when the view becomes part of the visible hierarchy — not on every re-render. Its pair, .onDisappear, fires when the view is removed.

options.text: When the view struct is initialized
When the view is first inserted into the visible hierarchy
Every time the view's body is re-evaluated
When the view moves offscreen

questions.explanation: layoutPriority determines which view keeps its ideal size when the stack must compress. Higher priority = last to shrink. Text A (priority 1) resists compression; B is compressed first.

options.text: Text A gets space preference; Text B is compressed or truncated if needed
Text B gets space preference because it is longer
Both texts get equal space
Compile error

questions.explanation: @Environment provides a read path for values placed in the view hierarchy with `.environment(_:_:)` or `.environmentObject`. It enables implicit dependency injection across deep view trees.

options.text: @Environment is for primitive values; @State is for objects
@Environment reads values injected by ancestor views (.environment modifier); @State is local to a single view
They are identical in behavior
@Environment owns the value; @State only reads it

questions.prompt: `some View` as a return type means…
questions.explanation: `some View` is an opaque return type — the compiler knows the exact type but hides it. Unlike `AnyView`, it preserves type information for optimization. The same concrete type must be returned on every path.

options.text: The return type is an existential — any view type at runtime
The return type is an opaque type — a specific concrete type the compiler infers, erasing its name but not its identity
The function can return different view types on different calls
It is equivalent to AnyView

questions.prompt: What is the difference between @StateObject and @ObservedObject?
questions.explanation: @StateObject ties the object's lifetime to the view — created once, persists until the view is destroyed. @ObservedObject just subscribes to changes on an already-existing object passed from outside.

options.text: They are interchangeable
@StateObject creates and owns the object (persists across re-renders); @ObservedObject receives an externally-owned object
@ObservedObject creates the object; @StateObject observes it
@StateObject is for value types; @ObservedObject for reference types
